en: Among the slain Chinese corpses,
Mighty Bakai kept looking.
“If I remain alive and do not die,
What inheritance shall I attain?
Parted from the lion favored by Khizr,
How can I go away alive?”
The horse he rode was Koktulpar;
The one he led was Arbuudan.
At that time Taibuurul
Was a horse just reaching maturity.
Fortunate Bakai the leopard
Was a man who never wearied.
Buurul, just reaching maturity,
Had its forelock tied with blue silk,
Its tail tied with pale silk,
Was covered with a bulletproof blanket,
And bore owl feathers on its head.
No father said, “I sired it”;
No mother said, “I bore it.”
Saikal, daughter of the renowned khan,
Had given Arbuudan as a gift.
Saikal, daughter of Khan Karacha,
Had presented Arbuudan as tribute.
Leading it, Bakai the revered master,
Shining in his coat of mail,
Leading Arbuudan by the rein—
Did you see him emerge from the hills,
King Bakai, radiant?
To his accomplished friend Manas
He brought Buurul and gave it.
To his renowned khan Manas
He gave Buurul as a gift.
When Chinese pressure and much torment
Befell him, he gave Buurul.
When turmoil no human had seen
Befell him, he gave Buurul.
When suffering no mortal had seen
Was borne by him, he gave Buurul.
When the precious lion held fast, motionless,
And the white saddle upon his shoulder
Was loaded, he gave Buurul.
When your Khan Manas endured suffering
Like this, he gave Buurul.
The reason he suffered was this:
Here Akkula had fallen to a bullet;
Here Almambet had died a martyr.
His wing had been broken;
He had lost the one he relied upon,
Parted from Khan Chubak.
Your warrior’s strength
Had been utterly spent.
Leaving him longing for one more sight,
He had died a martyr—
The son of Khan Ulak.
The edge of black steel,
Who had died a martyr in Beijing,
Was Syrgak, his trusted support.
For the warrior, the Blood-Shedding lord,
Parted from Akkula,
Had warrior Bakai not come,
It was the hour of capture.
Deeply grieving, the champion lion,
Leaning upon Akkelte,
Your warrior was overcome with sorrow.
The Black Chinese and many Manchus,
Learning of his distress,
Said, “I shall take him alive!”
And surrounded the leopard.
Entirely despairing of life,
Your ocean barely stood;
His companion and equal, Bakai the leopard,
Then reached your ocean-like hero.
“The fine white coat worn in battle—
Put it on, my precious friend!
Arbuudan can endure six months;
I have brought it as a gift.
Mount it, my champion lord!”
With care, Bakai the revered master
Kindled his extinguished fire.
As he stood helplessly on foot,
He revived the warrior’s deadened soul.
This was why he brought him back to life:
The stars had stirred in the sky;
Bakai and your Manas
Had become friends at six years old.
They had chewed white wheat flour together
And sworn upon the Holy Quran.
When his friend stood on foot,
Mountain-like Bakai, without delay,
Dismounted and ran to him,
Bending his knees to the earth.
Upon Arbuudan he set
The leather sweat-pad and white saddlecloth
That Kanykei had lovingly made,
The saddlecloth that fitted Arbuudan,
And the white saddle made by Almambet.
Its rear bow was solid silver,
Its two sides broad iron,
Skillfully fashioned from tempered steel.
Your companion Alma, your soul’s friend,
Had made it fit the leopard perfectly.
“When they crush him on a downward slope,
When your Magnanimous One braces his feet
And encounters many enemies,
His saddle might be shattered,
And in that desperate moment my Magnanimous One
Might meet an untimely death!”
Thus he made the exceptional white saddle,
The saddle fitted to Akkula.
When Manas took it and saddled
Buurul, just reaching maturity,
Sweat-pad against sweat-pad,
It was as though they had been measured together;
Crupper against crupper,
It was as though they had been cast together;
Girth against girth,
It was as though they had been fitted exactly.
Then renowned Manas
Hurriedly performed his prayers
And saddled the noble roan.
“The Black Kalmyks and Solons—
I shall drive them into Altai!
The dark unbelievers of Khangai—
I shall drive them toward Beijing!
If Kongurbay falls into my hands,
I shall capture him alive!
Karykan, lord of the imperial people,
I shall offer as a sacrifice!
My companions Alma and Chubak—
Thus I shall avenge them!”
Raging and thundering,
Manas the leopard roared.
His eyes blazed like a lion’s.
His precious teeth, broad as doors,
Your Khan Manas the leopard
Ground together again and again.
Wind burst from his mouth;
Blood came from his eyes as he stared.
When his true might was seen,
Those who looked lost their souls.
His thirst for blood had seized him.
For slaughter without retreat
The leopard was now preparing.
The battle-axe with golden cheeks
He slipped snugly onto his wrist.
Akkelte, which fired far away,
He now slung across his back.
Of the six blades descended from heaven,
Zulpuqor, which Manas had received,
When eagerly drawn from its sheath,
Never returned without drinking blood.
When swung in fury,
It never failed to wreak havoc.
When brought down upon a stone,
Not a notch remained upon its edge.
When it entered the fray, from its edge
Red blood swirled in a cloud.
When a mighty hostile enemy came,
And it was swung this way and that,
It gladdened his precious soul.
It cut off heads before the stroke was made.
Khan Manas’s Zulpuqor
He now fastened snugly at his waist.
With golden collar and copper sleeves,
Double mail with rings like larks’ eyes,
With a netted outer coat and ample jacket,
The splendid Akolpok,
With fine iron wire inserted,
Which wearied Kelte’s bullets,
Which no spear-point could pierce,
Which no arrowhead could penetrate—
The accomplished woman Kanykei
Had barely completed it in seven years.
Between Orenburg and Bukhara
She had the country searched.
The formidable woman Kanykei
Had fiber brought from there.
She had the fiber spun by the pood,
Spun in layers and worked together.
Filings of hardened steel
And siftings of fine sand,
Bound together with glue,
She had placed within its layers.
With iron inserted throughout,
Which defeated the enemy’s weapons.
Working it with consummate skill,
The exceptional woman Kanykei
Had fashioned it with ingenuity.
Taking no rest by day,
Taking no sleep by night,
From biting at the quilted armor
Her front teeth had grown weary.
From staring at the quilted armor
Her black eyes had grown strained.
The hardworking woman Kanykei
Had given to her champion Sultan Manas
Akolpok as a gift.
Mighty Manas stood towering
And now put on Akolpok.
Akkise, descended from heaven,
He flung around his waist with a cry.
A handspan of it was ridged,
A handspan of it was lacquered:
Your noble falcon’s lacquered spear.
If a fly landed, it rang;
If a whip-handle struck it,
It boomed like a war drum.
Furious, your Blood-Shedder
Took the lacquered spear in hand.
The banner fluttered in his hand;
Arkesken and his battle-axes
Glittered all about his body.
When he turned his front toward them,
He looked fearsome as a hungry lion;
When he turned his back toward them,
He took on the shape of a dragon.
Such was Manas the leopard, the warrior.
Parted from his champions,
His hour of slaughter had come.
The saintly elder, warrior Bakai,
Surged forward upon Koktulpar.
Beside Khan Manas,
Your gray-maned Bakai grew eager.
“Ajybai, son of Khan Argyn,
Old Kyrgyl, leader of the forty,
All forty of you, come here!”
He roared in fury.
Then Sultan Manas Khan
Called the forty champions:
“Damn your fathers’ graves, forty companions!
You forty were lions from forty lands.
‘They will serve in times of hardship,’
I thought as I kept you thus.
In the hollow of Zhylgynduu,
Along the broad Talas,
‘Whoever challenges us,’ you used to say,
‘If an enemy comes from a renowned land,
I shall smash Khangai,’ you used to say.
‘If a coveted, worthy enemy comes,
If a claim is made upon my precious head,
If someone will heed my words,
I shall bring him to terms,’ you used to say.
‘If I meet a man without religion,
I shall bring him into the faith,’ you used to say.
The hour for smashing has arrived!
With the Chinese people of forty tribes,
Warriors, the hour for mutual slaughter has come!
If a single gun gives a crack
And you take fright and run,
Warriors, that will mean your death at my hands.
If a black gun gives a bang
And you turn and run away,
I shall not count that man a support;
Mark me, that will mean your death at my hands.
When Allah Most High, the one God,
Issues his command,
